newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: WTO urges Brazil to resist domestic pressures.
newsitem.headline: WTO urges Brazil to resist domestic pressures.

text.p: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) urged Brazil on Thursday to give a "more measured response" to pressure from some domestic sectors for protection from imports.

In a report on Brazil's trade policies, the global trade watchdog also suggested Brazil's exchange rate might be overvalued, saying it could explain a sharp increase in imports since 1994 and a loss of export dynamism.
This scenario formed "the backdrop for recent moves to restrict selected imports and support exports", WTO said.
Brazil's automotive industry is the most highly assisted manufacturing activity in the huge country, with effective protection estimated at more than 250 per cent, it added.

Many of WTO's 125 member states, due to wind-up a debate on the report later in the day, were expected to express strong concern particularly over discriminatory protection in Brazil's automative, toy and textile sectors, according to trade sources.

"Greater co-ordination, transparency and a more measured response to requests for assistance from specific sectors would help Brazil translate its stated commitment to free trade into actions more clearly consistent with its development needs and with a strong multilateral trade system," WTO said.

"Today's challenge is to ensure the continuity of the more open, lower-inflation environment and preserve external balances, while achieving the rapid economic growth required to absorb an expanding labour force, and to resist pressure to reverse the reform process," it added.

Brazil has held bilateral consultations -- the first step in the WTO dispute settlement procedure -- with Japan, the United States, the European Union and South Korea who allege Brazil's car industry rules discriminate against imports.
No formal WTO dispute panel has been created yet to arbitrate in the automotive row -- but it appears inevitable unless Brazil can pacify its angry trading partners.

Brazil is a large net exporter of vehicles and its motor industry achieved record production levels in 1995, according to the WTO report. Tariffs on motor vehicles were increased to 70 per cent in March 1995 from 20 per cent in 1994.
"Under the automotive regime introduced in mid-1995, the industry benefits from tariff exemptions, combined with local-content and export balancing requirements," WTO said.
"In 1996, a certificate of compliance with Brazilian standards became mandatory to obtain an import licence for motor vehicles," it added.

Brazil's trade reforms were a key element behind its economic gains since 1992, although growth remained constrained by high real interest rates linked to tight monetary policies, according to the WTO report.
Under Brazil's tariff reform programme, its average applied tariff had dropped to 12.5 per cent from 21.2 per cent in January 1992, according to the report.
But it said that Brazil's adoption of MERCOSUL's common external tariff in January 1995 had not brought about improvement in its national tariff structure.
"Furthermore, frequent tariff adjustments give an apperance of uncertainty to Brazil's trade and investment regime."

WTO said that there had been a sharp appreciation of the real effective exchange rate after the new currency, the real, was introduced in 1994, but there has been a progressive depreciation since then.

"The possibility that the real effective exchange rate (REER) has been overvalued would be consistent with the sharp increase in imports since 1994 and a loss of export dynamism, which form the backdrop for recent moves to restrict selected imports and support exports," it said.
